highlights.text: Ibn Fāris derives ṭ-r-q from four base meanings: (1) arriving by night, (2) striking, (3) slackness/limpness, and (4) laying one thing over another
the star is called ṭāriq ("night-comer") because it rises at night
From this root he places ṭarīq (road), because it is trodden/come upon
ṭarīq also = palm-trees in one row (verse by al-Aʿshā)
**ṭrw — freshness/moistness**
Ṭarāwah/ṭarāʾah (verbal nouns of ṭariya – yaṭrā) = the state of being fresh/moist/new
al-buʿd is "distance / farness," the opposite of al-qurb ("nearness")
The adverb baʿdu ("after"), opposite of qablu ("before")
cf. Q. 11:83 «not far from the wrongdoers»
The prayer «our Lord, make the stages of our journeys far» (Q. 34:19) is read with both bāʿid and baʿʿid
He cites Imruʾ al-Qays, reading a phrase as yā buʿda mutaʾammal ("how far off is the thing one hopes for!") — a cry of regret
with a deathbed line by Mālik b. al-Rayb
بغى الشيء = to seek a thing, whether good or evil
ابتغى، تبغّى، استبغى all likewise mean "he sought it."
Ibn Sīda reads the Qur'anic "We did not teach him poetry, nor does it ينبغي for him" as "nor is it made easy/fitting for him."
بغى على فلان = he swerved from truth and overreached; = he rose against and wronged him
a verse of al-Aʿshā about gifting them (a free woman not being given as a gift) is cited
witness from Ṭufayl on scouts signalling the approach of a large army
Ibn Fāris analyses b-q-r as **two distinct roots**
The core sense is **بَقَرْتُ البطن (baqartu l-baṭn)**, "I slit the belly open."
**البقر (al-baqar)** is the collective noun of **البقرة (al-baqara)**, a single head of cattle
Ṭufayl: their playing-ground is "like the traces of the one who marks out circles"
**Sense group 1 — departure, emergence, coming into the open**
**Sense group 2 — intensity, severity, greatness**
مَا بَرِحْتُ أَفْعَلُ ذَلِكَ ("I have not ceased doing that") = "I still do it"
This is the sense in the Qur'anic citation {لَنْ نَبْرَحَ عَلَيْهِ عَاكِفِينَ} (Q 20:91, "we will never stop being devoted to it")
A slow riding-animal is cursed by its rider: "may you never move to good effect."
Cited from al-Aʿshā's poetry praising a lord and a neighbor as "great."
one root whose single idea is **stillness and staying put** — being motionless, and by extension continuing without break
دَامَ / يَدُومُ (dāma / yadūmu) = to become still. الماء الدائم (al-māʾ al-dāʾim) is standing, unmoving water.
Shāhid from al-Jaʿdī: "Their pot boils over against us, and we still it (nudīmuhā) … and cool it away from us when its heat rises."
an answer of ʿĀʾisha, asked about the Prophet's practice: "his practice was a dīma" — i.e. continuous
urgent, driven, often trembling haste — of people, animals, wind, spears, or flowing liquid
"and his people came to him, yuhraʿūn ilayhi" ("hurrying to him")
"and they, in the footsteps of their fathers, are yuhraʿūn" — meaning they run along hastily
Al-Muhalhil's verse: captives came "hurrying" (yuhraʿūn), led along in forced humiliation.
Ibn Aḥmar's verse: "I am not a hayraʿ... who flies off when the wind stirs him."
groups the root ج-ن-ب around the idea of the "side," and radiating from it, notions of nearness, being led at one's side, and being set apart / foreign
al-Janb — the side (of the body). "I sat at his janb" = "at his jānib," same sense.
jānabahu, tajānabahu, tajannabahu, ijtanabahu all mean to keep away from
jannaba/janaba a thing from someone = removed it far off — cited with Q 14:35, "keep me and my sons from worshipping idols."
al-jār al-junub = a neighbour who belongs to another people (a stranger-neighbour)
"the neighbour of janāba" = the neighbour who is a foreigner (shāhid from ʿAlqama b. ʿAbada, where janāba = remoteness)
treats this root as denoting hunger — emptiness of the belly — and its extension to intense longing
All signify hunger or emptiness of the belly, the contrary of شِبَعٌ (satiety)
Illustrated by the proverb أَجِعْ كَلْبَكَ يَتْبَعْكَ, "Make your dog hungry and he will follow you"
سَمَنُ كَلْبٍ بِجُوعِ أَهْلِهِ — "the dog grows fat by its owners' hunger,"
the suckling that creates the marriage bar is the one that answers an infant's hunger with milk, not the stage when only solid food would satisfy the child
the opposite of لؤم (baseness/meanness). It belongs to a man in his own person, even with no noble ancestry behind him
كَرُمَ (karuma), verbal nouns كَرَم and كَرَامَة, "to be/become noble." The agent is كريم (karīm)
أكرَمَ and كرَّمَ = to magnify and hold [someone] above reproach
In a line of Abū Dhuʾayb the reading كُرِّم ماءٌ صريحا is defended (against variant غُرِّم) by Abū Ḥanīfa as the sounder text
"to catch/snatch what is thrown": al-laqf is taking hold of something thrown at you, and specifically doing so swiftly
This is the sense the entry ties to the Qur'an: "fa-idhā hiya talaqqafu mā ya'fikūn" — "then it swallows up what they had fabricated"
Two verses by Abū Dhu'ayb are cited using laqīf of a trough that "crumbles" and "gushes forth."
a Ḥajj-related report has someone say "I caught (talaqqaftu) the talbiya-formula from the Prophet's own mouth,"
forbidding/restraining. النَّهْي (al-nahy) is the opposite of "command": to forbid.
تَناهَوْا عَن الشَّيْء: they forbade one another
النُّهْيَة، النِّهاية، النِّهاء: the furthest point and end of a thing — because its end "forbids" one from going further
النُّهَى (both singular and plural), النُّهْيَة، النِّهاية، المَنْهاة all = the intellect/reason
A line of Abū Dhuʾayb uses "my sight ended away from them" (with ʿan) to mean it was cut off from them
getting someone or something free. النَّقْذ (al-naqdh) is extrication, rescue, saving
أنقذه من فلان, استنقذه منه and تنقّذه all mean one thing — he saved him and got him clear
A horse you rescued and took back from an enemy
in Luqaym b. Aws al-Shaybānī's line — "Or was your thanks that, out of grudging, you made light of my rescuing you yesterday; would that I had not been there"
The core physical idea is pulling, drawing, or wresting something out.
To pull/wrest a thing from someone's hand; to draw it away.
نازعه / تنازعوا (to quarrel, munāzaʿa, nizāʿ)
Zamakhsharī cites Qur'an "And We drew forth from every community a witness."
تنازعوا الكأس (they passed the cup round); "the cup of slumber" was passed, i.e. drowsiness came on (verse of al-Shammākh)
with a verse of al-Nābigha comparing reined horses straining forward to birds fleeing a hailstorm
Core meaning: to sit.
qaʿada (verbal nouns quʿūd, maqʿad) = "he sat"; aqʿada = to seat/make another sit
qawāʿid al-bayt = a building's foundations
one who sits with you, a companion — as in Qur'an 50:17, "on the right and on the left a qaʿīd (seated one),"
an Arab oath, accusative verbal nouns governed by an implied verb, meaning "by your companion, the companion of every private converse,"
Hence the proverb "they made him qaʿīd al-ḥājāt" (their errand-drudge)
al-radd: turning a thing away and sending it back (verb raddahu / yarudduhu)
al-maradd = al-radd; irtaddahu = raddahu (turned/repelled it back)
irtadda / irtadda ʿanhu: to turn away or change from something
radīd = mardūd, "returned/rejected"
taraddada / tarādda: to go back and forth
A man miradd: much given to repelling and to renewed charging (shāhid from Abū Dhuʾayb)
Thaʿlab: the Day of Resurrection, since it cannot be turned back
Ḥadīth citation: the Prophet tells Surāqa b. Juʿshum that supporting "your daughter returned to you (mardūda), with no earner but you," is the best charity
it denotes one thing penetrating or passing into another
سَلَكَ (salaka) — to traverse a place or road (verbal nouns salk and sulūk). Transitively it means to make someone/something traverse or pass into a thing
كذلك سلكناه في قلوب المجرمين ("thus We made it pass into the hearts of the criminals") and فسلكه ينابيع في الأرض ("then He caused it to flow as springs in the earth")
سَلَكَ يَدَهُ في الجيب / السِّقاء — to insert one's hand into a pocket, waterskin, etc.
ʿAdī b. Zayd ("they routed you into a grievous affair") for salaka
Sāʿidah b. al-ʿAjlān ("they barred the road and drove them onto a lofty peak") for aslaka
derives the root from a core sense of nearness and treats "following/adjoining" as the thread running through its many derivatives
al-Walī = opposite of an enemy [ally/friend]
تَوَلَّى عنه = turned away; ولّى هارباً = turned in flight
Qur'anic shāhid: (ولكلِّ وِجهةٌ هو مُوَلِّيها) glossed as "facing it with his face."
the "fittest place" nuance with Labīd's مولى المخافة (the fittest seat of danger, with a note on how the line parses)
covers two groups of meaning: al-zinā (unlawful intercourse) with its forms and derived expressions, and a separate group built on narrowness and shortness
The article says the root sense of al-zanāʾ is narrowness
the Qur'an uses it: "and do not come near al-zinā" (Q 17:32)
The verb is zanā, yaznī, used of both man and woman
Al-Aʿshā's half-line "either marriage, or uzannu" is explained by some commentators as uzannī, "I commit zinā"
"Neither is her chastity chastity, nor her zinā zinā."
a ḥadīth forbids praying while zanāʾ, that is, while holding back urine
